title: Known by the one He blesses
hookLine: He is known by whom He chooses to be known (Sukhmani 16)

lines: NOT MILES ON A RUNNING APP.
cards: Five hundred days. If you've come this far, you've opened this path five hundred times, more than a year's worth of days. You might be tempted to think you've earned something: a level, a closeness, an understanding.
And in a way you have. You know words and stories you didn't know. But the sixteenth ashtpadi ends its salok with a line that gently turns the milestone around.
Knowing God, it says, isn't something you collect, like miles on a running app.

teach.b: Here's the end of the salok, in paraphrase: Nanak, He makes Himself understood to the one with whom He is pleased. Bujhaae: He causes to understand. Suprasann: well pleased, delighted.
So understanding God isn't seized. It's given, by the One, to whomever the One delights in.
The Sikh word for that giving is nadar: grace, the glance of favor, literally a look.

teach.h: KARMA THE GARMENT, NADAR THE GATE.
teach.b: Japji Sahib puts it in a well-known pair: by karma, by your actions, you receive this body like a garment; by nadar, by grace, you find the gate of liberation. Both halves matter. Actions are real and shape your life.
But the final door opens from the other side. That can sound unfair, as if effort doesn't count. Sikhs don't read it that way.
Look at how the tradition lives: rising early, reciting the banis, serving in the langar, remembering the Name all day. That's a lot of effort.
But the effort isn't a payment that buys grace. It's more like opening the curtains. You can't make the sun rise.

You can open the curtains every morning, so that when the light comes, it gets in. That's how many Sikhs describe their own daily discipline. The salok's grace is not a wage but a glance, given where the One is pleased.
The posture it points to is waiting with the curtains open: not grabbing, and not keeping score.

how: Sikhs speak of nadar, God's grace, as what finally opens the way, while keeping up daily effort in nitnem, seva and simran; the sixteenth salok of Sukhmani Sahib ends on this note.

o: grace, a glance of favor, given not bought
the reward earned after years of effort
a vow of silence kept for a whole day

games.q: known by grace — tap the pairs.

s: in this salok, understanding God is something you can collect by effort alone
the One makes Himself understood to whomever He delights in.
nadar literally means a look or glance
grace pictured as the One's glance of favor.
Sikhs read grace as making effort pointless
effort is like opening the curtains; it doesn't buy the light, but it lets it in.

games.q: you've practiced every day for five hundred days. by the sixteenth salok, what have you earned?
o: open curtains: readiness for a light that's given, not bought.
games.why: Japji says karma brings the garment, nadar the gate. effort keeps the curtains open; grace is the light.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up and open, and don't reach for any special feeling. Be like a room with the curtains open in the early morning, ready for whatever light comes and fine if it's still gray.
Each time you notice yourself straining, open your hands a little more; if you pray, let Waheguru be the only word, and let even that be quiet.

wordCard.voice: Nadar, grace, the glance of favor. The One makes Himself understood to whomever He delights in. Effort opens the curtains; nadar is the light.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nadar, grace, the glance of favor; a word from Persian nazar, sight.

carryVoice: Your line: known by grace. You can't make the sun rise, but the curtains are yours to open. Day five hundred, with thanks.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 16, salok (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 283)
Japji Sahib, pauri 4 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2)
